blocks.text: Landau lets himself be misled into his error (which Brecher also follows: Das Transcendentale, Magie und magische Heilarten p. 212, note 84) because that moth is also called elephant by some, and פלאי, or (as Aruch writes) פלייה, might be related to פיל (§. 173); but against these weak conjectures the explicit statement of the Talmud, which takes the צפורת כרמים as a species of locust of the genus of the ארבה, cannot be disregarded; we therefore believe we may rightly drop Landau's explanation**) and shall rather seek to identify a species of locust in our insect.

Conclusion. צפורת כרמים seems to us to be the locust species Gryllus stridulus (Voigt l. c. 5, p. 340). It is dark brown, the wing covers with lighter spots, the hind wings splendidly red, with a brown border at the end. The hind tibiae black, at the base with a yellowish crust.
It is common in summer and autumn on mountains and in forests. It flies up quickly and makes a rattling noise in doing so.

From all these features the names attributed to it by the Talmud can be explained. Aruch already remarks that פליה ביארי is a species of locust with which children are wont to play; that beautiful mixture of colours certainly makes our locust a little creature pleasing to children.

It may be called צפורת “bird” [p. 289] because of its quick flying up; כרמים means vineyards in particular, but already, like the biblical כרם, also any choice land laid out on rising ground; ציפורת כרמים thus means “bird of the mountains,” since our locust is frequently found on mountains*). The other name פלאי ביארי I translate: “piercing forests,” i.e. “devastating forests”; פלא means to ruin, to destroy (cf. the lexica) and בירי means forest (Buxdorf p. 1741); and indeed the Gryllus stridulus is just as destructive as the parent locust ארבה (§. 373).
A Species of Locust.
סלעם (Lev. 11, 22) is רשון (Chulin 65a), i.e. the biblical סלעם is called רשון in the vernacular. Aruch identifies the insect with רשנא, by which Onkelos renders כלעם; Jonatan has רשונא for it.
Ibn Esra derives the word from סלע “rock,” according to which סלעם is a rock locust, i.e. a locust dwelling on rocks.
Bochart (loc. cit. col. 446) takes סלע in the sense of בלע “to devour” and considers סלעם a voracious species of locust; Gesenius and Joh. Simon follow him. Accordingly סלעם is a migratory locust.

It should be noted that some call this locust not רשון but ניפול (Chulin 66a). Both names indicate the smallness of the locust. ניפול is also the name of the small bird, like Pullus, cf. §. 247, and רשון appears precisely as a designation of the smallness of an object; thus it is said: the human abortus is at the beginning of its formation the size of a רשון (Midr. R. Wajikra fol. 181, col. 1 and on this Tos. Nidda 25a. s.v. תחלת), and so we would have to think of a small voracious species of locust.

Conclusion. Here let the distinction be mentioned which the Tosephot make (Chulin 65b s.v. לא); according to it the ארבה (§. 373) is tailless and not humped on the forehead, the חרגול (§. 380) is humped and tailed, whereas the סלעם is tailless and humped.
The by-names רשון and ניפול (§. 376) are in some places also assigned to the חרגול; see §. 389 and Jonatan on Lev. 11, 22.
Related Genus.

To the genus of the סלעם the Talmud reckons the locust יוחנא ירושלמית (Chulin 65a); it is therefore, like סלעם, tailless, but humped on the forehead. As a clean locust it is permitted to be eaten. The epithet ירושלמית suggests that יוחנא too is gen. fem., and one might then think of the woman's name יוחני (a notorious sorceress; Sota 22a). It is not rare that animals are named after human names; one thinks of the glow-worm (Johanniswürmchen, "St. John's worm"), the St. Peter's fish, the Surinam Aeneas etc. Perhaps in this sense the bird names שבור אנדרפטא, פירח אנדרפתא (§. 185) and פרוא (§. 223) are also to be explained, since the Talmud (Chulin 62b) connects these names with men's names; פרוא too, it says there, was a sorcerer.

On the formation of human names from animal names see §. 109. Incidentally let it be remarked here that above p. 62 note ** we asserted that the Talmud only adds geographical epithets to the actual animal names but does not form the former after the homeland; this assertion is not contradicted by the name שפן (§. 152), since it is altogether improbable that the Hebrew word was formed from Spain; cf. above p. 110.
Related Genus.
To the genus of the סלעם the Talmud (Chulin 65b) further reckons the locust אושכף; like that one it is tailless and humped on the forehead between the antennae. It is permitted to be eaten.
Perhaps אושכף is corrupted for אוכף and is the saddle locust (Ephippigera). On the forehead there is a conical hump; however, the saddle locust is wingless and therefore cannot be clean.
The Grasshopper.

Bochart (loc. cit. col. 445) compares the Hebrew חרגול (Lev. 11, 22) with the Arabic حَرْجَلٌ [ḥarjalun], which in Arabic means a swarm of locusts. حَرْجَل [ḥarjal] means to hop, to gallop, which is why Gesenius translates it as grasshopper (Heupferd, "hay-horse"). This is the common grasshopper [p. 291] (Locusta viridissima). Green, with wings lying parallel, twice as long as the body, the wing spot of the back brown, the ovipositor straight. With the wings over 2 inches long (Voigt l. c. 5. p. 332).
This locust is called ניפול (§. 377) in some places, in others רשון (ibid.; Chulin 65a). It is tailed and humped on the head (§. 377).
The egg of the חרגול was worn in the ear as a remedy against earache (Sabbat 67a). It may be eaten.
The pl. of חרגול is חרגולי; thus it says in the Sulat for the 1st Sabbath of Chanuca (s.v. אין צור): טסו חרגולי ילק “The Chargole and the Jelek came flying.”
